content.text:
You're working in our DurHack repo (https://github.com/LB17GO/HotDrones), HotDrones: TypeScript + Vite, no 3D yet. It's a working top-down 2D sim of a firefighting drone swarm that keeps coordinating when comms fail, built for the Neptune North "Actors work better together" challenge. Your job is to freeze the current 2D version in a `BASIC/` folder, turn the main app into an isometric 3D version in a Smashy Road-like style with every feature from our spec, and wire in the sponsor and MLH tools from step 4 in ways judges will actually see in the demo. It has to look great live, and the headless experiments behind our pitch have to keep working.

Read README.md, `Project Overview:` and everything in src/ and scripts/ before changing anything (about 2,000 lines). Work on a new branch `iso-3d`, commit after each step with a clear message, push as you go so the team can pull it, and keep `npm run dev` demoable at every commit. Make sensible calls without asking unless you're genuinely blocked, and log them in DECISIONS.md. If time runs short, steps 1 and 2 are the must-haves, then 3, then Tiger Data, Gemini and ElevenLabs from step 4, then the rest of 4, then 5. Always leave time for step 6.

## Working with Entire
We're entering MLH's "Best Use of Entire", so your session is being captured and linked to commits. Check with `entire status`; if it isn't enabled, run `entire enable`, `entire plugin install graph` and `entire graph init-agents`, and ask me to finish `entire login --device`.
- Use `entire graph search --query "..."` (add `--repo .` if it asks) to find code before grepping or opening whole files.
- At the end of each step, record the decisions and lessons as a brain checkpoint (check docs.entire.io for the current command) as well as in DECISIONS.md, so later sessions don't undo working code.
- Push often so teammates' agents can resume from your checkpoints. If the repo is mirrored on entire.io, open a Trail per step so a teammate's agent can review it.

## Ground rules
- `src/sim/` stays pure TypeScript with no Three.js, DOM or network imports, so `npm run experiment` keeps running in Node.
- Renderers and integrations only read world state and never call `world.rng` or `world.agentRng`. Cosmetic randomness like tree placement comes from a hash of the tile index. The only writes are judge actions, which all go through one function that also records them with their tick for replays.
- Every new sim behaviour is a config option, and anything random gets its own RNG stream. With all of them switched off (e.g. a `--legacy` flag on the experiment script), `npm run experiment` must reproduce the committed `results/summary.csv` exactly; diff it after step 3 to prove the sim didn't drift.
- Network calls never block a tick. They're async, rate-limited and fire-and-forget from the sim's point of view.

## 1. Snapshot the 2D version into BASIC/
- Start with `git mv "Project Overview:" PROJECT_OVERVIEW.md`, because a colon in a filename breaks checkout on Windows.
- Copy the app as it stands into `BASIC/`: index.html, src/, scripts/, results/, package.json, package-lock.json, tsconfig.json, .gitignore and README.md, without node_modules or dist. It must run standalone with `cd BASIC && npm install && npm run dev`.
- Add root scripts `dev:basic` (BASIC/ on its own port, using the root node_modules, so both versions can run side by side) and `experiment:basic` (runs from inside BASIC/ so its results land in BASIC/results/, never the root).
- Open BASIC/README.md with a line saying this is the frozen 2D version and isn't edited any more.
- Commit, and tag it `v-2d-basic`.

## 2. Isometric 3D renderer
Add `three` and `@types/three`. Build the renderer in `src/render/iso/`, split by concern (scene and camera, terrain, trees, fire and smoke, drones, overlays, picking) so a few of us can work on it in parallel. Keep `src/render/renderer.ts` and reuse it as a small 2D minimap in a corner, showing the truth or the selected drone's belief.

Go for a Smashy Road-like look: chunky voxel/low-poly, flat-shaded with no textures, bold saturated colours, crisp directional shadows, toy-like, all geometry built from primitives with no external assets. Use an orthographic isometric camera with drag to pan, wheel to zoom, Q/E to rotate 90° (hills hide things) and a reset button.
- Each tile is a box column at its sim height, with a coloured top cap over earthy sides, using InstancedMesh throughout. `terrain.height` runs about 0–24 with 1 tile = 1 unit, so apply one vertical scale (start around 0.4) to everything: terrain, drone altitude (terrain + `droneAltitude`), the base mast (+6), link endpoints and smoke. That way links visibly clear or clip hills exactly where the sim's line-of-sight test says.
- Grass is bright green, forest darker green with 1–3 low-poly conifers per tile, sand pale yellow, rock grey with a boulder, and water flat blue with a gentle shimmer (the sim already flattens water).
- Burning tiles get flickering emissive voxel flames sized by `env.severity` (1–3). Burning trees lose foliage and turn charcoal, and burnt tiles go dark with the odd ember. Extinguished tiles are `Burnt` with wetness 1 (wetness only decays on unburnt tiles), so show them wet and dark, distinct from burnt-out ground. Wetted unburnt tiles get a faint blue tint.
- `env.smoke` drives grey semi-transparent low-poly puffs over each tile, opacity by density, drifting with `env.wind` (angle is the direction it blows towards, speed 0–1).
- The village's nine tiles become small houses with pitched coloured roofs that char if they burn. The base is a helipad with a radio mast that goes dark when `world.baseOnline` is false.
- Drones are tiny quadcopters with spinning rotors, body colour by state (reuse the 2D state colours), an ID label and small water, battery and damage bars, flying at their sim altitude. When a drone's `waterDropped` goes up, blue voxels fall and steam puffs if the tile was burning. Dead drones fall and leave a smoking wreck.
- Blackout zones are translucent purple domes, and usable links are glowing lines between nodes at altitude.

The current loop runs 1–12 whole ticks per animation frame, which reads as jumpy and far too fast in 3D. Replace it with a ticks-per-second control that goes slow enough to watch (around 5–30) up to the current maximum, add single-step, and interpolate drone positions between ticks.

Port every existing control and panel: mode, seed, new run, play/pause, the judge tools (select, start fire, blackout, crash drone), wind sliders, comms range, cut base comms, clear blackouts, smoke-blocks-comms, the view toggles, the selected drone's map with staleness fog, teammate guess clouds, sensor ring, selected-drone panel, stats and chart. Picking raycasts the pointer to a tile (instanceId → tile index) and then reuses the existing tool logic. Add a wind compass, a banner when the village is lost (the sim keeps running after that; don't change `World.finished`, the experiments rely on it), an end card when the run finishes (burnt area, village status, drones lost, water dropped, time to extinguish, plus replay and new-seed buttons), and a tile inspector for clicks that don't land near a drone.

Diff the fire and wetness arrays each tick and only update instances that changed. Hold 60 fps on a laptop with 10 drones on the 64×64 map.

## 3. Spec gaps in the sim
Each of these is a config option. Choose the defaults the 3D app should use, and give each one a visual.
- Smoke should need several burning tiles. On the current model, one isolated burning forest tile in calm wind peaks at about 1.7 smoke (grass about 1.2), above `thickSmoke` (0.8) and the comms-block level (1.2), while wind of 0.3 or more keeps it under 0.6. Make thick smoke impossible from a single tile at any wind speed.
- Smoke blocks comms by default, since the spec treats smoke between drones as infinite distance. Keep the toggle.
- Descending drains battery too, not just climbing.
- Add a drone-count slider (applied on New run) and an option to spawn the drones in a line on the pad.
- Add a pure function to comms.ts that says why a pair within range can't link (hill, smoke or blackout) without changing `canLink`. Draw those pairs as dashed links coloured by reason, so judges can watch links snap as drones go behind hills or into smoke.

## 4. Sponsor and MLH integrations
Everything here lives outside `src/sim/`. Add a small Node + TypeScript server in `server/` (HTTP API plus WebSocket, proxied by Vite in dev; in production it serves the built app) and a client layer in `src/integrations/`. The client layer derives one typed event stream by diffing world state each tick: fire spotted by the base, drone state changes, crashes, links lost and regained, base offline, village threatened or lost, fire out, and judge actions. The radio log, voices, AI commander, databases and ledger all consume that stream. Secrets live in a gitignored `.env` with a committed `.env.example`; only the server reads them, and nothing secret goes in the browser bundle. Each integration switches itself off when its key is missing and shows a status dot in the UI, so the demo still works offline on bad hackathon Wi-Fi.
- Tiger Data (Tiger Cloud: Postgres + TimescaleDB) is our live database. Create hypertables for drone telemetry (position, altitude, state, battery, damage, water), fire metrics (burning, burnt, thick-smoke tiles, comms groups, links, base online) and events, with `time` set to run start + tick seconds so `time_bucket` works for live and experiment runs alike. The browser batches telemetry to the server about once a second. Add continuous aggregates and a columnstore/compression policy, and build a `dashboard.html` page that reads from the aggregates: the live run (fire growth, connectivity, battery spread) and the experiment comparison (swarm vs central vs greedy across comms range). `npm run experiment -- --db` streams runs into the same database (downsampled, e.g. every 10 ticks, to stay inside the free tier), so the dashboard fills in while a sweep runs.
- Gemini (`@google/genai`, current Flash model, e.g. `gemini-3.8-flash`) is an AI incident commander at the base, and it only sees what the base knows: the zones `computeZones` finds on the base's belief map, which drones are in the base's comms group right now, and the last status heard from the rest. Every 20–30 seconds of wall-clock time, or on a major event, it writes a short radio-style sitrep for the radio log, labelled with how stale its information is. It takes typed or spoken judge commands through function calling, mapped onto the existing judge tools (start a fire, place a blackout, crash a drone, set wind, cut base comms), and shows a confirm chip before running any action. At the end of a run it writes an after-action report from the event log and the metrics in Tiger Data. It advises humans and drives judge tools only, never the drones, so the decentralised claim stays honest. When base comms are cut its sitreps visibly go stale, which is part of the pitch.
- ElevenLabs (`@elevenlabs/elevenlabs-js`) gives the sim its sound. Gemini's sitreps and key alerts are read out in a dispatcher voice. Drone radio calls (low battery, returning to base, refilling, lost link, crashed) use a few distinct voices, are pre-generated per drone and event, cached, and played through a radio filter (band-pass and squelch). A script, `npm run audio:generate`, uses the Sound Effects and Music APIs to make rotor, fire, splash, steam, crash, wind and squelch sounds plus calm, tense, critical, victory and defeat music stems in `public/audio/`, committed so the demo needs no network; the music crossfades with the threat level. Optionally add push-to-talk judge commands using ElevenLabs speech-to-text feeding Gemini.
- DurHack's theme is Composition, so make the swarm audible too. In a Web Audio layer each drone is a voice pitched by its ID, and drones that can reach each other play on a shared beat. A group that gets cut off drifts out of time and detunes, then snaps back into sync when it reconnects, so you can hear the network split and heal. Fire intensity drives the percussion.
- MongoDB Atlas stores scenarios and replays as documents. Because the sim is deterministic, seed + config + the recorded judge actions replay a run exactly, so save scenarios with a shareable `?scenario=<id>` link. Add a "Challenge the swarm" board: when someone saves a scenario, the server runs it headless in every mode (the sim already runs in Node), stores the outcomes and Gemini's after-action report, and ranks the scenarios that hurt the swarm most.
- Vultr hosts the demo and runs the big experiments. Add a Dockerfile and docker-compose (server plus built app behind HTTPS, e.g. Caddy) and deploy notes for a Vultr Cloud Compute instance. Give the experiment runner a `--workers N` option (worker_threads), and document a large sweep (e.g. 300 seeds per condition) on a high-CPU Vultr instance streaming into Tiger Data.


## 5. CBBA and forecasting (stretch)
- Add a `cbba` mode alongside the existing `swarm` auction, which stays as it is. Each drone builds a bundle of up to about 3 zones (the zone for its current load, then the next ones after refills) using time-discounted marginal scores, and drones run CBBA consensus (Choi, Brunet & How, 2009) on zone slots (zoneId#k) over the live network. Reuse the particle-filter tracker for teammates out of contact, as swarm mode does.
- Optionally let drones forecast the fire by running the spread model forward from their own belief map, and bid on where the front will be.

## 6. Experiments, README, CHALLENGES.md and DEV post
Add conditions for smoke blocking comms on and off, regrowth, towers and the `cbba` mode. Re-run `npm run experiment` with the new defaults, then update the README results table, the report and the run instructions (3D app, `dev:basic`, `experiment:basic`, the server and `.env.example`). Write CHALLENGES.md mapping every challenge we could enter (Neptune North, RS Group, Waterstons, Accenture, and the MLH Gemini, ElevenLabs, Tiger Data, MongoDB Atlas, Vultr, Solana and Entire prizes) to the features and files that address it, with a 30-second demo script for each. Draft `docs/dev-post.md` for the MLH DEV writing challenge: the story, architecture, results charts and what we learned.

## If there's time
- Add a compare view that runs the same seed in two modes side by side (e.g. swarm vs central), each in its own viewport. Seed 15 is our best demo.
- Add vitest tests for determinism (same seed, same metrics), newest-wins map merging, a hill blocking line of sight, and regrowth only next to healthy vegetation. (make no mistakes ahah)w

1	# HotDrones
2	
3	A swarm of firefighting drones that keeps working when communications fail.
4	Built for the **Neptune North "Actors work better together"** challenge at DurHack 2026.
5	
6	A wildfire spreads across hilly coniferous forest towards a village. Ten drones carry water from lakes to the fire front. Hills, distance and blackout zones cut their radio links, and the home base can go offline. Every drone makes its own decisions from its own map. When drones can talk, they merge what they know and agree who fights where. When they can't, each one guesses where its lost teammates probably are and works around them.
7	
8	## Run it
9	
10	```bash
11	npm install
12	npm run dev          # opens the simulation in the browser (http://localhost:5173)
13	npm run experiment   # headless: 30 seeds x every condition -> results/ (about 2.5 min)
14	npm run typecheck
15	```
16	
17	Open `results/report.html` after running the experiments for the charts.
18	
19	## Results (30 random maps per condition)
20	
21	| Condition | Swarm (ours) | Central control | No coordination | No drones |
22	|---|---|---|---|---|
23	| Perfect comms (range ∞) | 935 burnt, village lost 20% | 1001 burnt, 17% | 2067 burnt, 57% | 3077, 100% |
24	| Normal comms (range 14) | **887 burnt, 13%** | 2281 burnt, 73% | 2163 burnt, 63% | 3077, 100% |
25	| Poor comms (range 6) | **1073 burnt, 20%** | 2808 burnt, 97% | 2175 burnt, 60% | 3077, 100% |
26	| Base offline at tick 120 | **890 burnt, 13%** | 2585 burnt, 83% | 2128 burnt, 63% | 3077, 100% |
27	
28	**The pitch in one line:** with perfect comms, a central controller and our swarm do about equally well. As soon as comms degrade, central control collapses and the swarm barely notices.
29	
30	Every approach faces exactly the same fires on each seed (fire randomness and drone randomness use separate generators), so the comparison is fair.
31	
32	## How it works
33	
34	```
35	src/sim/            the simulation: no graphics, runs in the browser AND in Node
36	  config.ts         every tunable number in one place
37	  rng.ts            seeded random numbers (reproducible runs)
38	  terrain.ts        hills (value noise), tile types, village, base
39	  environment.ts    the TRUE world: fire spread, severity, water, smoke, wind
40	  belief.ts         a drone's private fire map + tile-by-tile merging
41	  comms.ts          who can talk: range, 3D line of sight over hills, blackouts, relaying
42	  planner.ts        turning the believed fire front into task zones with threat scores
43	  tracker.ts        particle filter guessing where lost teammates are
44	  drone.ts          one drone: sensing, flying, battery, damage
45	  world.ts          the tick loop, the auction, the baselines, judge controls
46	src/render/         top-down canvas renderer (swap in an isometric one here)
47	src/main.ts         browser UI and controls
48	scripts/experiment.ts  headless experiment runner -> CSV + HTML charts
49	```
50	
51	### Each tick
52	
53	1. **Environment:** wind drifts; fire spreads, intensifies and burns out; smoke drifts downwind and fades.
54	2. **Sense:** each drone observes tiles within its sensor radius. Thick smoke shrinks that radius.
55	3. **Network:** work out which drones (and the base) can reach each other.
56	4. **Share:** everyone in the same connected group merges fire maps and plans.
57	5. **Track:** each drone updates its guesses about teammates it can't hear.
58	6. **Act:** each drone refuels or recharges if needed, otherwise picks and flies to a target and drops water.
59	
60	### The fire
61	
62	Each tile is grass, forest, sand, rock or water. Only grass and forest burn. Every tick a burning tile can ignite each of its 8 neighbours with probability
63	
64	`spreadBase × fuel × wind × slope × severity × (1 − wetness)`
65	
66	- **wind:** `exp(strength × speed × cos(angle between wind and spread direction))`, so fire races downwind;
67	- **slope:** `exp(0.25 × height difference)`, so fire runs uphill;
68	- **severity** rises the longer a tile burns (1 to 3). Hotter fires spread faster and need more water;
69	- **wetness:** water dropped on unburnt ground makes it hard to ignite for a while (firebreaks);
70	- **embers:** very hot fires occasionally throw a spot fire a few tiles downwind.
71	
72	The fire burns for 60 ticks before the drones are called out, so they face an established fire.
73	
74	### What a drone knows
75	
76	Drones **never read the true world**. Each has a `BeliefMap`: for every tile, what it believes (unburnt / burning / burnt) and *when it last saw it*. It learns from its own sensor and from other drones. Maps are merged **tile by tile, newest observation wins**, so partial maps from different drones combine correctly. In the UI, *Show selected drone's map* displays one drone's belief, darkened where it is out of date.
77	
78	### Who can talk to whom
79	
80	Two nodes can talk if they are within radio range, neither is in a blackout zone, and the straight 3D line between them (at flying altitude) clears the hills. Messages relay through other drones, so a whole connected group shares information. Smoke does not block radio by default, because in reality it barely affects it, but there is a toggle. The base has a taller mast and a longer range. Docking at base swaps maps by cable even when base radio is down.
81	
82	### Choosing what to fight: the auction
83	
84	1. **Task zones.** The drone finds the *front* on its own map (burning tiles next to unburnt fuel) and groups it into 6×6 zones. Burning tiles in the middle of the fire are ignored because they'll burn out anyway.
85	2. **Threat score** for each front tile: `severity × closeness to the village × wind pushing it towards the village × fuel ahead`. A zone's value is the sum, with a bonus for small spot fires that can be fully put out. Zones are worth 1 to 4 drones ("slots") depending on size.
86	3. **Bid** = `zone value ÷ time to make an impact` (including a detour to refill if the drone is empty), plus a small stickiness bonus for its current zone so drones don't dither.
87	4. **Consensus.** Drones in contact share claims: who is going where, with what bid. A drone takes the best zone that isn't already full of teammates with *higher* bids. This is a consensus-based auction in the style of CBAA (Choi, Brunet & How, 2009). Higher bids always win and ties go to the lower ID, so drones that can talk settle on a conflict-free split.
88	
89	### When a teammate goes quiet: the particle filter
90	
91	When a drone stops hearing from a teammate, it creates 40 guesses (particles) at the teammate's last known position. Each tick they fly towards the teammate's last known target with some randomness, so the cloud spreads the longer the silence lasts. When deciding whether a zone is already covered, a lost teammate counts as
92	
93	`exp(−time since contact / 120) × fraction of guesses near that zone`
94	
95	A recently lost teammate is trusted to still be doing its job. One silent for a long time, or possibly crashed, gradually stops counting, and the drone covers its zone itself. When contact returns, the cloud collapses back to the real position. Select a drone in the UI to see its clouds.
96	
97	### Staying alive
98	
99	- **Battery** drains every tick, faster flying into a headwind or climbing. A drone heads home when it has just enough charge to make it back, with a safety margin.
100	- **Damage** builds up from flying over fire and through smoke. Above 70% the drone goes home for repair. At 100% it is destroyed.
101	- **Water:** 5 drops per load. Empty drones fly to the water source that minimises the detour to their target.
102	- **No fire on the map:** fly home to fetch the base's map. If that has none either, **scout** areas nobody has seen for a while.
103	
104	### The baselines
105	
106	- **Central control:** the base assigns every drone it can reach using the same scoring, so it's a strong baseline when comms are good. Drones out of contact finish their last order and fly home for new ones. Peer-to-peer map sharing is off.
107	- **No coordination:** each drone goes for its own best zone and ignores the others' plans. Maps are still shared, so this isolates the value of the auction itself.
108	
109	## Judge controls (in the browser)
110	
111	- **Start fire:** click to ignite a tile.
112	- **Comms blackout:** click to place a zone where radios don't work.
113	- **Crash drone:** click a drone to destroy it.
114	- **Cut base comms:** take the base offline.
115	- **Wind direction and speed** sliders; **comms range** slider; **smoke blocks comms** toggle.
116	- **Select a drone** to see its state, who it can reach, its top zone bids, and its guesses about lost teammates.
117	
118	Seed 15 is a good demo: the swarm saves the village; central control and no coordination both lose it.
119	
120	## Ideas for next steps
121	
122	- Isometric renderer (keep `src/sim` untouched; add `src/render/isometric.ts`).
123	- Full CBBA (each drone plans a sequence of zones instead of one).
124	- Fire forecasting inside each drone: run the fire model forward from its belief and target where the fire *will be*.
125	- Real elevation data for a real wildfire-prone area.

--- README ---
# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at http://127.0.0.1:35469
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
/root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:35469/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active
   (javaTrustStorePath, toolTrustFailureCodes, gitSshRewrite,
   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at /root/.ccr/ca-bundle.crt
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present,
  JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS points JVMs at a truststore that holds the proxy CA: the
  JDK's own store if the system trust install already added the CA there,
  otherwise /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit"). Confirm
  javaTrustStorePath is set in the status output before pointing a build at it
  (toolTrustFailureCodes explains why it is missing). If the image or the
  build sets its own trustStore, that one wins — import the proxy CA into it
  with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

Most often the destination host is not allowed for this session. Do not retry
or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the status endpoint
records the reason.

### 429 / 503 from the proxy

Too many connections or requests went through the proxy, or the egress proxy
was busy. The proxy can hold a connection for about a minute before it refuses
it, so a tool with a short timeout of its own may report only a timeout. Run
fewer downloads or requests at once, then retry. connectsWaitingForTunnel and
openTunnels in the status output show the load. busyTunnels includes idle
connections until one has to wait, so alone it does not show load, and it can
pass maxBusyTunnels.

### "connection reset" / "unexpected disconnect" / "RPC failed" mid-transfer

Once a tunnel is up the proxy cannot send an error response, so a connection
it aborts (tunnel to the egress proxy lost, or an upload the tunnel stopped
accepting) reaches the tool as a bare reset. recentRelayFailures in the status
output names the host and reason; check it before concluding the remote
service refused the operation.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

# Entire repository agent guide — Graph

Use Graph for code discovery, structural understanding, and semantic change analysis.
Use Graph EVERY time you need to find code or a code relationship, not only at the
start. Your first action on a task that requires finding code MUST be a Graph query,
and each later locate or relationship question MUST also go through Graph:

    entire graph query --repo . --profile full --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --query "<task>"
    entire graph def --repo . --head --max-context-bytes 4096 <Name>
    entire graph neighbors --repo . --head --format agent --max-context-bytes 4096 --symbol <Name> --direction in
    entire graph impact --repo . --head --max-context-bytes 4096 --symbol <Name>

query finds the code for a description. def shows what a named symbol is.
neighbors lists callers (--direction in) or callees (--direction out). impact gives
the blast radius before you change a symbol. Use these, not grep, for definitions,
callers, references and dependents. Use grep/rg only for literal strings, config
keys, environment-variable names and file names.

--head reads the committed tree from a cache. Drop --head only when the answer
depends on uncommitted edits. The first call in a large repository can take tens of
seconds while that cache loads; later calls take about a second. Run the command
directly: it needs no timeout wrapper, and macOS has no timeout command.
A Coverage or Completeness line lists files Graph could not parse, often minified or
generated ones. It does not mean the results are partial; only a failure in the
language you asked about can hide a fact, and then you check that one relation in
source. Static relations can be incomplete: an empty result is not proof of no callers.

This holds for small edits, follow-up work, and tasks that already name the file.
A named file answers where code is; it does not answer what else depends on it.
Do not skip the query on the grounds that the available context feels sufficient.
Use Graph diff, commit, and checkpoint for semantic comparisons of code revisions.

Inspect the source Graph displays at useful locations before editing. A result marked [complete]
certifies a structurally whole displayed body, unchanged by rendering, for the source
view observed by that query. It does not certify dependencies, later source freshness,
or task resolution. Do not reread the same unchanged span merely to duplicate it.
The marker never waives a read your editing tool requires before it changes a file:
when the tool requires one, perform that read. If you cannot establish that a span is
unchanged since the query, treat it as changed and read it.
An unmarked result is not certified: it may be a partial window or a whole body whose
marker did not fit. Retrieve only the specific additional span, surrounding context,
caller, contract, or second site required for the task. If edits, formatting, generation,
checkout, or another writer may have changed the relevant source, verify that current
span before reusing remembered output. A --head result does not cover working-tree
changes absent from that snapshot. Check related contracts
and make the smallest complete change. VERIFY before stopping: execute focused tests,
a reproduction, or the most relevant build. If execution is unavailable, disclose
